1	# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya
2	
3	> Status: v3 after 17 independent review rounds; approved by the owner 2026-11-09 · Updated: 2026-11-09
4	> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
5	> what it gives Compliance.
6	
7	## How to read this
8	
9	Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
10	Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
11	auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.
12	
13	| Marker | Meaning |
14	|---|---|
15	| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
16	| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
17	| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
18	| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
19	
20	Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
21	**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
22	14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
23	(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
24	`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
25	Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".
26	
27	---
28	
29	## 1. The decision in one page
30	
31	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
32	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
33	
34	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
35	
36	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
37	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
38	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
39	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
40	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
41	
42	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
43	|---|---|
44	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
45	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
46	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
47	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
48	
49	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
50	
51	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
52	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
53	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
54	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
55	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
56	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
57	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
58	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
59	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
60	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
61	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
62	  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
63	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
64	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
65	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
66	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
67	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
68	  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
69	  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
70	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
71	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
72	- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
73	  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
74	  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
75	  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
76	  for speed.
77	- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no CloudTrail for k0s changes
78	  (so S3 reconciliation does not cover them), and no break-glass when Actions is down (G1, G2).
79	- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
80	  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
81	  unavailable" for JIT. Their keys and hosting are open (G19).
82	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
83	  business associate, as the brief implies.
84	
85	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
86	
87	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
88	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
89	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
90	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
91	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.
92	
93	### Roles
94	
95	| Role | Rule |
96	|---|---|

# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya

> Status: v3 after 17 independent review rounds; approved by the owner 2026-11-09 · Updated: 2026-11-09
> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
> what it gives Compliance.

## How to read this

Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |

Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".

---

## 1. The decision in one page

Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.

**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):

1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |

**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**

- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
  for speed.
- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no CloudTrail for k0s changes
  (so S3 reconciliation does not cover them), and no break-glass when Actions is down (G1, G2).
- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
  unavailable" for JIT. Their keys and hosting are open (G19).
- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
  business associate, as the brief implies.

**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):

1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.

### Roles

| Role | Rule |
|---|---|
| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
| L3 owner team | Owns the process-defining L3 paths and the SCP stack (layer 3); composition open (G17). |

---

## Layer 1 — Identity and access

**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default

39	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].

63	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.

# 01 — Đóng khung bài toán (problem framing)

## English summary

- **Main problems:** engineers run Claude Code on laptops with SSO profiles that reach production, some with permission
  prompts off; MCP servers/plugins are installed without review; CI uses long-lived GitHub tokens and AWS keys; on-call
  and monitoring are fragmented. Grouped into 7 areas: identity & access, production change paths, agent behaviour,
  tooling supply chain, sensitive/tenant data, detection & evidence, security of agent-written code (§1).
- **Central conflict:** Engineering and Compliance only truly conflict on *writes to production*; reading real data
  (medical, national ID, bank) is a grey zone (§3). Security of Papaya's production AI agents is out of scope (§1.4).
- **Key assumptions (owner-confirmed, §4):** separate prod/non-prod AWS accounts with IAM Identity Center; GitHub Team
  plan (no environment reviewers on private repos, no merge queue); laptops are untrusted; every prod change is approved
  before apply, incidents included; agents read metadata only, real data by approved exception; the approver is never the
  author or the authoring agent; non-prod holds synthetic data only.
- **Success criteria (§5):** zero long-lived prod-write credentials on laptops or in GitHub secrets; zero unapproved or
  after-the-fact prod changes; no loss of engineer speed (approval wait ≤ 1 h in working hours, free non-prod loop);
  incident approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7; audit evidence for any prod change within 30 min; plus managed agent config,
  a reviewed plugin catalogue, approved-only access to real data, CI security checks on agent code, no real data in non-prod.

> Working note (Vietnamese). Mục đích: hiểu đúng bài toán **trước** khi nghĩ giải pháp.
> File này cố ý **không đề xuất giải pháp**. Mọi dữ kiện về Papaya lấy từ `work/00-challenge.md`;
> những gì đề không nói được tách riêng ở mục 4 và đánh dấu **[GĐ]** (giả định).
>
> Updated: 2026-11-08 · Status: giả định và phạm vi đã được người dùng xác nhận qua 2 vòng hỏi (mục 6)

Ký hiệu nguồn (theo Rule 1 trong `CLAUDE.md`):
- **[Đề]** dữ kiện có trong đề bài (`work/00-challenge.md`), đã đọc trong phiên này ✅.
- **[GĐ-n]** giả định, xem mục 4.
- ⚠️ nhận định về khả năng của công cụ chưa kiểm chứng; sẽ kiểm ở bước thiết kế.

Ký hiệu loại dữ liệu bị ảnh hưởng: **MED** hồ sơ y tế / chẩn đoán / lịch sử claim · **NID** CCCD / national ID ·
**BANK** tài khoản ngân hàng · **TEN** cách ly giữa các tenant (insurer partner, nhiều quốc gia).

---

## 5. Tiêu chí thành công

Đo được, có cách đo, có mục tiêu. Các số mục tiêu đã được xác nhận ở mục 6.

| # | Tiêu chí | Cách đo | Mục tiêu |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Không còn credential dài hạn có quyền ghi prod trên laptop. | Số IAM user/access key có quyền ghi vào account prod; số quyền ghi prod gán thường trực cho người. | **0** |
| S2 | Không còn credential cloud dài hạn trong GitHub secrets. | Số AWS access key, GitHub PAT, Firebase/GCP key dài hạn được workflow dùng. | **0** |
| S3 | Mọi thay đổi prod, kể cả trong sự cố, có một người duyệt có tên, khác người làm, **trước** khi áp dụng. | Đối chiếu định kỳ (hằng tháng) các sự kiện ghi trong log cloud của prod với bản ghi phê duyệt. Đếm số thay đổi không khớp, và số thay đổi có thời điểm duyệt sau thời điểm áp dụng. | **0** / **0** |
| S4 | Engineer không mất tốc độ. | (a) Thời gian từ PR được tạo tới khi thay đổi hạ tầng chuẩn lên prod (median). (b) Thời gian chờ duyệt (median). (c) Vòng lặp ở non-prod không có bước duyệt mới. | (a) trong cùng ngày làm việc; (b) ≤ 1 giờ trong giờ làm việc; (c) đúng |
| S5 | Mọi cấu hình agent dùng trên máy engineer là cấu hình được duyệt. | % máy engineer nhận chính sách Claude Code của tổ chức; số engineer có thể tắt toàn bộ permission prompt mà không ai biết. | **100%** / **0** (phụ thuộc GĐ-6) |
| S6 | Mọi MCP server/plugin đang dùng nằm trong danh mục đã duyệt, và việc duyệt không thành nút cổ chai. | Số MCP/plugin đang dùng ngoài danh mục; thời gian xử lý yêu cầu thêm mới. | **0** ngoài danh mục; xử lý ≤ 5 ngày làm việc |
| S7 | Phát hiện và phản ứng có chủ, và sự cố không bị kẹt vì chờ duyệt. | Có lịch on-call có tên, gồm cả người duyệt; mọi alert prod về một kênh định tuyến; thời gian chờ duyệt cho thay đổi trong sự cố (24/7). | Lịch on-call có tên; 100% alert prod qua một kênh; chờ duyệt trong sự cố ≤ 15 phút, 24/7 (cần ít nhất primary + backup trực duyệt) |
| S8 | Evidence cho audit lấy ra nhanh. | Với một thay đổi prod chọn ngẫu nhiên: thời gian để trình ra đủ "ai đề xuất, ai duyệt, đã duyệt cái gì, cái gì được áp dụng, khi nào". | ≤ 30 phút, không cần hỏi người liên quan |
| S9 | Đọc dữ liệu thật trên prod chỉ xảy ra qua ngoại lệ được duyệt. | Số phiên agent/người đọc MED/NID/BANK trên prod không có yêu cầu được duyệt kèm theo; mọi yêu cầu có thời hạn và phạm vi tenant. | **0** phiên không có yêu cầu được duyệt |
| S10 | Code do agent viết đi qua cùng guardrail với code người viết, trước khi tới nhánh deploy. | % PR vào nhánh deploy có secret scan, kiểm tra dependency và SAST chạy và đạt; số lần push thẳng lên nhánh deploy; số secret bị phát hiện **sau** khi merge. | **100%** / **0** / **0** |
| S11 | Non-prod không chứa dữ liệu thật (GĐ-14). | Số lần copy dữ liệu prod xuống non-prod; kết quả quét định kỳ dữ liệu nhạy cảm trên non-prod. | **0** |

S4 ngang hàng với các tiêu chí bảo mật một cách có chủ đích. Nếu S1–S3 đạt nhưng S4 không đạt, P3b
cho thấy engineer sẽ đi đường vòng, và S1–S3 sẽ không giữ được lâu.

---

## 6. Câu hỏi kiểm tra lại (đã trả lời)

### Vòng 1

Người dùng trả lời trong chat, session 2 (2026-11-08).

| # | Câu hỏi | Đề xuất | Quyết định của người dùng |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Quy mô đội (GĐ-1) | 20–60 engineer, DevSecOps 1–2 người, không một reviewer duy nhất | Đồng ý |
| 2 | Reviewer khác tác giả? (GĐ-11) | Có (four-eyes); agent không là reviewer | Đồng ý, reviewer không phải người làm (tác giả hoặc agent tạo thay đổi). Hỏi lại: agent độc lập chỉ là bước review tự động bổ sung; phê duyệt chính thức phải là người |
| 3 | Agent đọc dữ liệu thật? (GĐ-9) | Không, cho tới khi có thoả thuận | Đồng ý mặc định là không; **cho phép theo từng trường hợp** khi có thoả thuận phù hợp, vì có lúc debug cần dữ liệu thật |
| 4 | Thay đổi khẩn cấp chưa duyệt? (GĐ-8) | Có, với 4 điều kiện và review sau | **Không đồng ý.** Mọi thay đổi prod phải được duyệt **trước**, kể cả trong sự cố |
| 5 | Ép cấu hình agent? (GĐ-6) | Laptop không tin cậy; kiểm soát chính ở cloud/CI | Đồng ý |
| 6 | Mục tiêu tốc độ (S4) | Duyệt ≤ 1 giờ trong giờ làm việc; ship trong ngày | Đồng ý |
| 7 | Phạm vi | Nguyên tắc chung cho tất cả; chi tiết cho AWS + GitHub Actions; GCP, k0s, Firebase ở mức áp dụng nguyên tắc | Đồng ý |
| 8 | Ưu tiên 30 ngày | (1) bỏ credential dài hạn trong CI, (2) thu hẹp quyền prod thường trực, (3) danh mục MCP/plugin | Đồng ý; on-call và monitoring ở giai đoạn 2 |

### Hệ quả cần mang sang bước thiết kế

- **Mâu thuẫn giữa câu 4 và câu 8.** Không có break-glass thì sự cố nào cũng cần một người duyệt có mặt ngay, 24/7.
  Nhưng on-call (P7) lại được xếp ở giai đoạn 2. Trong 30 ngày đầu, nếu thu hẹp quyền prod (ưu tiên 2) mà chưa có
  người duyệt trực, sự cố ngoài giờ có thể bị kẹt. Cần chọn một trong hai: (a) đưa "danh sách người duyệt trực"
  (chỉ phần tối thiểu của on-call) lên giai đoạn 1, hoặc (b) chỉ thu hẹp quyền prod sau khi có người duyệt trực.
  **Đã quyết (a):** đưa phần tối thiểu "danh sách người duyệt trực" (có tên, phủ 24/7) lên giai đoạn 1,
  làm trước hoặc cùng lúc với việc thu hẹp quyền prod. Phần còn lại của on-call và monitoring vẫn ở giai đoạn 2.
- **Câu 3** cần một đường xin quyền đọc dữ liệu thật, khác với đường xin thay đổi, và có thêm điều kiện là
  thoả thuận/hợp đồng cho phép. Thêm tiêu chí S9.
- **Câu 4** chuyển rủi ro P7b từ "có người đi đường tắt" thành "sự cố kéo dài vì chờ duyệt". S7 đổi thành đo thời gian chờ duyệt trong sự cố.

Người dùng trả lời trong chat, session 3 (2026-11-08). Mỗi câu hỏi có một đề xuất; người dùng chọn đề xuất ở tất cả các câu.

## Layer 1 — Identity and access

**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
  holds.
- **Process rules** that follow from this:
  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
    accepted as a process control, D2);
  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
    research 6.9.4 Q2);
  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
    TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b) or a small home-built flow (⚠️ R2.4.2) on the documented APIs
    `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2);
  - no standing prod-write permission set.
- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
    JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); protect the org trail (📖 R2.6.2).
  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path, held by the L3 owner team only, not co-owned by the on-call group; OD13).
- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).

**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1); CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` /
`DeleteAccountAssignment` per grant (📖 R2.4.2), linked to its approval by request ID [design]; SCPs
and trust policies as Pulumi code; IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on policy PRs
(📖 R2.8.1; from phase 2); quarterly access review of permission sets and GitHub admins.

**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write and keep a free non-prod loop. Prod reads stay
fast for metrics and metadata, but shrink during the transition: because the engineer's access is the
agent's access, from phase 1 the engineer too loses raw logs and configuration of services not yet
redacted or moved to runtime secrets. Configuration values come from the IaC code instead (layer 1
above); raw logs that may hold customer data need an L3-data grant. The data owner is not on the
on-call schedule, so at night the grant is approved by the on-call approver alone and the data owner
reviews it the next working day [design]; the wait still counts against S7. This is
the largest cost of the first months. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.

---

183	## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls
184	
185	**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
186	and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
187	untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).
188	
189	**On Papaya's stack**
190	
191	- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
192	  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
193	  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
194	- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset in layer 8 ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`, `forceLoginOrgUUID`, the `ask` rule for WebFetch, and the other deny rules) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):
195	
196	  | Key | Value and reason |
197	  |---|---|
198	  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
199	  | `permissions.allow` | Read-only commands Papaya uses, to cut prompts (R6.9.3). It contains no command listed in `sandbox.excludedCommands` (`aws`, `pulumi`, `serverless`): an allowed excluded command would run outside the sandbox, with `~/.aws` and the network, without a prompt (⚠️ inference from R1.2.6, R1.6.4) [design]. Cost: a prompt for every `aws` read. |
200	  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, research 6.9.4 Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
201	  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes bypass mode (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode, where a classifier approves instead of a person, stays available (D1) and is measured through `permission_mode`. |
202	  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. The HIPAA template denies WebFetch (R5.5.4); "ask" is a deliberate deviation so that documentation lookups still work. |
203	  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.285 for `allowedProviders` (R1.1.15), which also covers `--restricted` (2.1.248, R6.9.1b) and the plugin-pin fix (2.1.179, R6.2.7); ≥ 2.1.295 if any managed hook uses `onFailure: "block"` (R1.5.2); and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
204	  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). `forceLoginOrgUUID` checks claude.ai sign-ins only, not Claude Console sign-ins (R5.5.5); with it set, sessions on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are refused (R1.11.3.11). |
205	  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
206	  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`; `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws`, which the sandbox can otherwise read (R1.6.3, R1.6.4). |
207	  | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` | Left at its default `true` (owner decision OD12). This widens D1's "Manual + read-only allowlist": every sandboxed command, writes in the working directory and calls to allowed domains included, runs without a prompt. Detail: sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, so in Manual mode prompts are for edits, unsandboxed commands and fetches, not every command (R5.5.5b). A deliberate choice: the sandbox (no `~/.aws`, allowlisted network) is the control for those commands. The HIPAA README says to set `false` if policy needs a person to approve each command (R5.5.5b); cost of `false`: a prompt per command. |
208	  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
209	  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |
210	
211	- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, the plan is to
212	  list `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
213	  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), which likely includes the network (⚠️ inference). How the list matches
214	  commands (prefix or text, and chained commands) is not researched (⚠️). This is worse than an
215	  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
216	  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
217	  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
218	  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
219	  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
220	  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
221	  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
222	  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
223	  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
224	  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
225	  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
226	  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
227	  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
228	  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
229	  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
230	  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
231	  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
232	  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
233	  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
234	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
235	- **Session types:**
236	
237	  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
238	  |---|---|---|---|
239	  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
240	  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, research 6.9.4 Q1–Q2). No WebFetch, and file tools confined to the working directory (📖 R6.9.1b); Edit/Write are excluded only if `--tools` acts as an exclusive list (⚠️ unverified), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
241	  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, research 6.9.4 Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
242	  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
243	  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |
244	
245	- **Phase-1 interim posture:** the sandbox and credential denies arrive in phase 2 (OD4), so for
246	  the first 30–60 days `~/.aws` is readable and the network is open to every Bash command; in auto
247	  mode the classifier is the only gate. Impact is bounded once standing prod write is removed at the
248	  end of phase 1 (layer 1); before that, today's exposure continues, and token theft is easier in this window.
249	- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless
250	  `"onFailure": "block"` (📖 R1.5.2); `--restricted` cannot be forced by a setting (📖 R6.9.1), and a `PATH` wrapper on laptops can be bypassed (⚠️ R6.9.1c);
251	  on laptops **without MDM**, a different login, an API key or a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variable skips
252	  server-managed settings, `allowedProviders` included (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ R1.8 #3, G11). So S5's
253	  "nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed" is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
254	- **Auto memory:** engineers review it and delete it after a suspicious session; residual risk with a
255	  named owner (D3).
256	- **Fallback:** switch to `disableAutoMode` (📖 R1.2.2) if the planted-injection test steers auto mode, a serious
257	  advisory appears, or an audit finds auto mode touched a protected scope (D1).
258	
259	**Audit evidence.** Managed settings as an expected copy in git with PR approvals. The live copy is
260	edited in the Claude admin console by Owners / Primary Owners (📖 R1.1.5), not by PR, and Team audit
261	events for settings changes are unconfirmed (⚠️ R1.1.12). `/status` shows which managed source
262	applies (📖 R1.1.18), and likely not the key values (⚠️), so it cannot detect a console edit; until a way to read the
263	live values is found (G18), an Owner exports the console settings monthly and diffs them with git
264	[design], and the list of Claude org Owners is kept short and reviewed quarterly; `/status` and `claude doctor` from
265	sampled machines (📖 R1.1.18); OTel `claude_code.tool_decision` (`permission_mode`) and
266	`claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user` (`duration_ms`, rubber-stamping signal) (fields 📖 research 6.6
267	D1 metrics; thresholds ⚠️).
268	
269	**Cost / value.** More prompts than auto mode, partly offset by the read-only allowlist. Compliance
270	gets one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices (P3c).
271	
272	---
273	
274	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
275	
276	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
277	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
278	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Every prod change needs two people, and
279	no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it; the on-call backup only replaces an
280	unavailable primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how
281	many. Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
282	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Confirmed by the owner
283	(OD13): the original author opens the approval PR and the first approver
284	approves it. If the first approver is unavailable, another owner of the stack approves; that makes
285	three people and is recorded as a deviation, counted monthly (OD11). A cross-team PR needs one
286	approval, as GitHub accepts one on-call group member for files of several owner teams (OD10,
287	OD9, 📖 R3.2.7); domain review there is a recommendation, counted in the monthly report. A real-data read is not a change and has its own rule, L3-data. Incidents use the same
288	path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
289	
290	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
291	|---|---|---|---|---|
292	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
293	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (needs state-write permission on a DIY S3 backend, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |
294	| **L2** | Routine prod change in code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, release | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → `main` → deploy workflow |
295	| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM/SCP; replace/delete of stateful resources; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/**`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, plugin/MCP catalogue and the rest of the canonical list in layer 5; advisory policy finding | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher. L3 paths (workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, the SCP stack): the L3 owner team only (OD13); IAM-only stacks are deployable, so the L3 owner team plus the on-call group (OD9). L3 content inside a domain file (an IAM statement in `serverless.yml`, a stateful delete): the stack's owner, then the risk stop (OD8). In incidents: the on-call approver for deployable paths (OD9); paths that define the process (CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, workflows) wait for the L3 owner team | same path; for IaC changes the risk stop also applies; workflow and agent-config files have no prod diff |
296	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b); incidents only, as the owner accepted it (Options §9 Q2); the on-call approver counts as owner of the service in the request (OD13) | layer 7 |
297	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |
298	
299	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for
300	the whole team (OD3). With code-owner review on, every PR, L2 included, needs an approval from an
301	owner of the files it touches (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7; per-file behaviour ⚠️ not a separate research row).
302	What differs at L3 is **which team** owns the path: L3 paths are owned in CODEOWNERS by a designated
303	L3 owner team (deployable L3 paths also by the on-call group, OD9), L2 paths by their domain team; and IaC changes at L3 meet the
304	risk stop. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files, so they are approved by
305	the stack's owners, not the L3 team (OD8); automated checks make up for this: IAM Access Analyzer
306	`check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and the Pulumi policy pack (📖 R4.2.2), both from phase 2 (layer 5). Cost: changes to `CLAUDE.md` (where D3 puts shared knowledge) need the L3 owner team, not
307	the domain team that edits it most.
308	
309	**On Papaya's stack**
310	
311	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
312	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
313	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
314	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is
315	  no merge queue (⚠️ R4.6 #1; whether updating drops approvals is open, Options §8).
316	- **L3 approvals [design]:** CODEOWNERS plus code-owner review only, no path-based required
317	  reviewers rule. That rule (📖 R3.2.4) asks for approvals from specific teams, which the on-call
318	  group would not satisfy at night, and how it combines several teams is not researched (⚠️), so it
319	  would break OD9 or add a third person. GitHub stops the author from approving (📖 R3.3.1). A required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5), set by a dedicated GitHub App that reacts to review events and is the pinned source [design; hosting, key storage and whether its key counts against S2 are not researched, ⚠️ G19], adds what
320	  the rules cannot: for app-opened PRs it excludes the person who triggered the agent, and it counts
321	  only human approvals, since an app's approval might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3). A workflow
322	  instead of an app is weaker: pinning the source to GitHub Actions likely lets any workflow set a
323	  check of the same name, and the trigger that runs on review events from trusted code is not
324	  researched (⚠️ G19).
325	- **Who approves at night (OD9):** a fixed GitHub team with write permission (owners without it
326	  are silently not assigned, 📖 R3.2.7; the CODEOWNERS validation check covers this), the on-call approvers, is listed as
327	  co-owner on every deployable path in CODEOWNERS (infrastructure and service code), next to the
328	  domain team. Confirmed by the owner (OD13): the group does **not** co-own the paths that
329	  define the process (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md` and agent config, catalogue); those stay
330	  with the L3 owner team only. If a broken workflow blocks a night fix, the pipeline counts as
331	  unavailable and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7). One primary and one backup from that team are on call. Technically any member can approve any
332	  path; by rule the primary approves and the backup only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
333	  Membership is fixed, not changed per shift [design]. GitHub team membership is set in organization
334	  settings, not by a PR; managing it as code (e.g. with Pulumi's GitHub provider) and the audit
335	  event for a membership change are not researched (⚠️ G16). Meanwhile the layer-7 settings
336	  comparison includes the group's member list. Cost: an approval from any
337	  listed owner satisfies code-owner review (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days a member could approve
338	  another domain's PR, on or off shift. Mitigation [design]: process rule "approve another
339	  domain's PR only if it carries the `incident` label and you are on shift", and a monthly report of
340	  every cross-domain approval by group members on PRs without that label (layer 7). Whether Papaya's team size allows full coverage is unknown
341	  (§1, S7).
342	- **Risk stop [design]:** applies to every deploy, whatever the level. The deploy job previews prod;
343	  on stateful replace/delete, an IAM change, a network or security-group change, or an advisory
344	  policy finding (from phase 2) it stops and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a second PR that adds
345	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` (`<sha>` = the stopped commit) holding that SHA and the
346	  preview hash; the workflow does not open it, because the setting that lets Actions create and approve PRs stays
347	  off (📖 R3.3.3; ⚠️ R3.6 #3). CODEOWNERS on `deploy-approvals/<stack>/` names the owners of that stack and the
348	  on-call group (OD8, OD9). The approver is ≠ author and may be the first PR's approver, who now sees
349	  the prod diff. Merging it triggers the deploy on the new HEAD, which previews again and continues
350	  only if the hash matches the approved one; if another PR merged in between, the hash differs and
351	  the deploy stops again (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8). Cost: while a stack is
352	  stopped, later merges to that stack stop too until a matching approval lands; in an incident, a
353	  risky change already waiting on `main` blocks the fix for the same stack until it is approved or
354	  reverted. A
355	  `mandatory` policy violation always blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2): the fix is a code change, or a
356	  change to the policy pack through its own L3 PR. Preview output is filtered for
357	  outputs and secrets before it is posted (Options §1; ⚠️ R4.6 #2).
358	- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if (⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c): `production`
359	  allows only `main`; only the reusable deploy workflow (under CODEOWNERS) references it; no ref/SHA
360	  inputs; no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers; one concurrency group
361	  per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
362	- **Pulumi:** PRs preview non-prod only, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
363	  secret access (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). On `main`: prod preview, then `pulumi up` with the
364	  policy pack, which stops on a mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2). Prod runs allow no `--skip-preview`
365	  (📖 R4.1.2) and no targeting, replace, `state`, `import`, `destroy` (⚠️ R4.6 #3, G12). Pulumi Cloud,
366	  if used: OIDC via `pulumi/auth-actions`, no stored token (📖 R4.1.4).
367	- **Serverless v4:** `serverless package`; `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI
368	  because differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2); `serverless deploy --package`
369	  (📖 R4.4.3); a least-privilege `deploymentRole`, which cannot be removed later and is usable by
370	  anyone who may operate the stack (📖 R4.4.5), so JIT roles get no stack-operation rights.
371	- **State:** writable by deploy roles (and possibly the drift role, layer 7); Pulumi
372	  secrets via `awskms` on a DIY backend (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #7).
373	- **k0s [design]:** manifests in the monorepo, applied by CI; no write RBAC for humans or agents in
374	  prod; read roles exclude logs and exec in namespaces with claim data (mechanism: G1). The risk
375	  stop is described for Pulumi and Serverless only; for k0s manifests (RBAC changes are the IAM
376	  equivalent) a `kubectl diff`-based stop is a candidate, not researched (⚠️ G1). Firebase deploys
377	  have no preview step in this design (⚠️ G2).
378	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only
379	  slow unrelated tests skipped [design]. A required check skipped by a path filter may stay
380	  pending and block the merge (open, Options §8); this directly affects S7.
381	
382	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
383	
384	The incident responder is engineer E; the on-call approver is R (a backup replaces R only if R is
385	unavailable).
386	
387	1. E's incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
388	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
389	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
390	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as E.
391	3. R, a co-owner of `serverless.yml` through the on-call group (OD9), reviews the diff. If R
392	   catches a missing queue change, R does not fix it (OD7): E pushes the fix, the stale approval is
393	   dismissed, and R approves again, one more review round (Options §6). E merges.
394	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
395	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
396	
397	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks); run log and preview artifact, exported because
398	retention is unverified (⚠️ G7); deploy-role CloudTrail events; all linked by commit SHA and run ID.
399	
400	**Cost / value.** One approver for every prod change, from the owners of the path; two approvals,
401	usually by the same approver, when the risk stop fires (OD13; OD11). Cross-team PRs: one approval (OD10). None in non-prod.
402	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.
403	
404	---
405	
406	## Layer 4 — Supply chain for MCP servers and plugins
407	
408	**Principle.** Local MCP servers, plugins and hooks run with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5); remote MCP servers receive tokens and data.
409	Only reviewed, pinned entries from a catalogue are allowed. The catalogue is the inventory (P4c).
410	Review takes ≤ 5 working days (S6), or people work around it.
411	
412	**On Papaya's stack**
413	
414	- **Plugins:** a private marketplace repo with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (📖 R1.4.1), sources
415	  pinned to `ref`/`sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only). Managed `strictKnownMarketplaces` = Papaya only,
416	  `blockedMarketplaces`, `enabledPlugins: false` to pull one (📖 R1.4.2), checked before download and
417	  at session start (📖 R1.4.3). `disableSideloadFlags` rejects `--plugin-dir`, `--plugin-url`,
418	  `--agents`, `--mcp-config` but not `.mcp.json` or `claude mcp add` (📖 R1.4.2). With
419	  `allowManagedHooksOnly`, plugin hooks run only for force-enabled plugins (📖 R1.5.4). User mods are
420	  blocked by the `allowManagedModsOnly` option under `pluginConfigs` → `cc-plugin-sec-default@builtin`
421	  → `options` (📖 R1.5.6). The version floor covers the plugin-pin fix of 2.1.179 (📖 R6.2.7).
422	- **MCP:** "approved catalogue" = `allowedMcpServers` + `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true`; without
423	  the lock users can widen it (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4). Match by `serverUrl` or `serverCommand`, never
424	  `serverName` ("not a security control", 📖 R1.3.3); `serverCommand` matches the exact argv (📖 R1.3.3), so the catalogue entry pins an exact package version in it [design].
425	  `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7). With MDM, `managed-mcp.json` gives exclusive control;
426	  it cannot come from server-managed settings (📖 R1.3.2).
427	- **Review checklist** [design]: publisher; local `stdio` or remote (📖 R6.4.3); what it reads and where
428	  it sends data, with a supplier-register entry and BAA/DPA status (⚠️ R5.6); no token passthrough
429	  (📖 R6.4.2); write tools for Slack, Linear, GitHub only where needed (⚠️ R6.5 #6); how the server authenticates (Linear and Slack: G9); pinned version,
430	  reviewer, date.
431	- **Known gaps:** no per-group targeting in server-managed settings (📖 R1.1.6, R1.4.4); tool
432	  description changes after approval are not covered (⚠️ research 6.6).
433	
434	**Audit evidence.** Catalogue file in git (each entry = an approved PR); supplier register; OTel
435	`claude_code.plugin_installed` / `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6). MCP tool logging needs
436	`OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` (📖 R1.3.8); it stays off until we know whether it logs tool inputs (⚠️).
437	
438	**Cost / value.** Up to 5 days' wait for a new tool. Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier
439	records.
440	
441	---
442	
443	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
444	
445	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
446	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
447	checks as human code (S10).
448	
449	**On Papaya's stack**
450	
451	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
452	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
453	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
454	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
455	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
456	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
457	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
458	  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
459	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
460	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
461	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
462	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
463	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
464	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
465	    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
466	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
467	    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
468	    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
469	    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
470	    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
471	  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
472	  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
473	  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
474	    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets
475	    [design].
476	
477	  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
478	  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
479	  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to
480	  add or remove nodes, live in the cluster, not in GitHub; they follow layer 1 (no static keys, a
481	  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
482	- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
483	  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
484	- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
485	  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (availability on Team ⚠️); the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so
486	  the deploy workflow lives in the same repo (📖 R3.5.5; conclusion [design]).
487	- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,
488	  `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, `.devcontainer/` (📖 R3.2.8; list ⚠️ R6.5 #5, R6.3.11), plus
489	  `.npmrc` (registry redirection) [design], the policy packs, the SCP code and the
490	  catalogue file. This is the canonical L3 path list that layer 3 refers to. Not on it:
491	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/`, owned by the stack's owners and the on-call group (OD8, OD9). The private plugin
492	  marketplace is a separate repo and needs its own ruleset and CODEOWNERS [design]. CI validates the file, because
493	  invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7).
494	- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code** (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` + checkout,
495	  📖 R3.5.4).
496	- **Agent review:** an independent agent (not the one that made the change) may post an automated
497	  review as an extra check; it never counts as an approval (GĐ-11).
498	- **Agents in CI:** `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues, Pull
499	  requests (📖 R1.7.8), whose own credentials are listed in the S2 inventory (⚠️ G19); Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token (📖 R1.7.6);
500	  `--restricted` and explicit `--tools` (D3; passing it through `claude_args` unverified, ⚠️ research
501	  6.9.4 Q5); a managed-settings file on the runner, which also guards against mods (📖 R1.5.6; for
502	  federation auth ⚠️); MCP set fixed by CI because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
503	  (📖 R1.3.5); never `environment: production` (⚠️ R3.6 #4). Hosted runners give `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1),
504	  so with `Bash` in `--tools` the runner file is advisory (⚠️ R3.5.1, R3.6 #4).
505	- **App-opened PRs:** a required check set by a dedicated GitHub App, pinned as its source (layer 3), confirms at least one approval by a
506	  human who did not trigger the run; counting approvals is not enough, since the app's own approval
507	  might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3; 📖 R3.2.5).
508	- **Required checks (S10):** from phase 1, secret scanning, dependency check, SAST (products: G4);
509	  from phase 2, IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and Pulumi policy packs
510	  (📖 R4.2.2). For Serverless stacks, Access Analyzer would check the IAM policies in the
511	  CloudFormation template that `serverless package` produces, against the deployed ones (⚠️ not
512	  researched); policy packs do not apply to them. Until phase 2, the only compensation for OD8 is
513	  the risk stop, which fires on every IAM change in the prod preview.
514	
515	**Audit evidence.** Workflows and lockfile in git; audit-log events such as
516	`org.update_actions_secret`, `repo.set_workflow_permission_can_approve_pr`, `repository_ruleset.update`
517	(📖 R3.3.3, R3.5.6). An audit event for environment-secret changes was not researched (⚠️); the
518	settings comparison in layer 7 covers the S2 exception meanwhile. Check results per PR; secrets inventory (S2).
519	
520	**Cost / value.** One-time migration to OIDC and pinned actions; slower action updates. Compliance
521	gets S2 and the same guardrails for agent and human code.
522	
523	---
524	
525	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
526	
527	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).

## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls

**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset in layer 8 ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`, `forceLoginOrgUUID`, the `ask` rule for WebFetch, and the other deny rules) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):

  | Key | Value and reason |
  |---|---|
  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
  | `permissions.allow` | Read-only commands Papaya uses, to cut prompts (R6.9.3). It contains no command listed in `sandbox.excludedCommands` (`aws`, `pulumi`, `serverless`): an allowed excluded command would run outside the sandbox, with `~/.aws` and the network, without a prompt (⚠️ inference from R1.2.6, R1.6.4) [design]. Cost: a prompt for every `aws` read. |
  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, research 6.9.4 Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes bypass mode (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode, where a classifier approves instead of a person, stays available (D1) and is measured through `permission_mode`. |
  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. The HIPAA template denies WebFetch (R5.5.4); "ask" is a deliberate deviation so that documentation lookups still work. |
  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.285 for `allowedProviders` (R1.1.15), which also covers `--restricted` (2.1.248, R6.9.1b) and the plugin-pin fix (2.1.179, R6.2.7); ≥ 2.1.295 if any managed hook uses `onFailure: "block"` (R1.5.2); and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). `forceLoginOrgUUID` checks claude.ai sign-ins only, not Claude Console sign-ins (R5.5.5); with it set, sessions on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are refused (R1.11.3.11). |
  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`; `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws`, which the sandbox can otherwise read (R1.6.3, R1.6.4). |
  | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` | Left at its default `true` (owner decision OD12). This widens D1's "Manual + read-only allowlist": every sandboxed command, writes in the working directory and calls to allowed domains included, runs without a prompt. Detail: sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, so in Manual mode prompts are for edits, unsandboxed commands and fetches, not every command (R5.5.5b). A deliberate choice: the sandbox (no `~/.aws`, allowlisted network) is the control for those commands. The HIPAA README says to set `false` if policy needs a person to approve each command (R5.5.5b); cost of `false`: a prompt per command. |
  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |

- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, the plan is to
  list `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), which likely includes the network (⚠️ inference). How the list matches
  commands (prefix or text, and chained commands) is not researched (⚠️). This is worse than an
  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
- **Session types:**

  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, research 6.9.4 Q1–Q2). No WebFetch, and file tools confined to the working directory (📖 R6.9.1b); Edit/Write are excluded only if `--tools` acts as an exclusive list (⚠️ unverified), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, research 6.9.4 Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |

- **Phase-1 interim posture:** the sandbox and credential denies arrive in phase 2 (OD4), so for
  the first 30–60 days `~/.aws` is readable and the network is open to every Bash command; in auto
  mode the classifier is the only gate. Impact is bounded once standing prod write is removed at the
  end of phase 1 (layer 1); before that, today's exposure continues, and token theft is easier in this window.
- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless
  `"onFailure": "block"` (📖 R1.5.2); `--restricted` cannot be forced by a setting (📖 R6.9.1), and a `PATH` wrapper on laptops can be bypassed (⚠️ R6.9.1c);
  on laptops **without MDM**, a different login, an API key or a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variable skips
  server-managed settings, `allowedProviders` included (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ R1.8 #3, G11). So S5's
  "nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed" is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
- **Auto memory:** engineers review it and delete it after a suspicious session; residual risk with a
  named owner (D3).
- **Fallback:** switch to `disableAutoMode` (📖 R1.2.2) if the planted-injection test steers auto mode, a serious
  advisory appears, or an audit finds auto mode touched a protected scope (D1).

**Audit evidence.** Managed settings as an expected copy in git with PR approvals. The live copy is
edited in the Claude admin console by Owners / Primary Owners (📖 R1.1.5), not by PR, and Team audit
events for settings changes are unconfirmed (⚠️ R1.1.12). `/status` shows which managed source
applies (📖 R1.1.18), and likely not the key values (⚠️), so it cannot detect a console edit; until a way to read the
live values is found (G18), an Owner exports the console settings monthly and diffs them with git
[design], and the list of Claude org Owners is kept short and reviewed quarterly; `/status` and `claude doctor` from
sampled machines (📖 R1.1.18); OTel `claude_code.tool_decision` (`permission_mode`) and
`claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user` (`duration_ms`, rubber-stamping signal) (fields 📖 research 6.6
D1 metrics; thresholds ⚠️).

**Cost / value.** More prompts than auto mode, partly offset by the read-only allowlist. Compliance
gets one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices (P3c).
